title: TB1-12014
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "male claimant"), his wife XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "claimant" herein unless otherwise indicated) and their minor children, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, are citizens of China. They claim protection under Sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 ALLEGATIONS (From amended common PIF Narrative of adult female claimant (the "claimant" herein unless otherwise indicated) in Exhibit C-2):

The claimant had her first daughter on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2004, and could not have a second child until she waited 4 years and got a permit. She was forced to wear an IUD, which she had problems with, and she was forced to have two abortions when it was discovered she was pregnant in XXXX 2006 and XXXX 2007. She had a second daughter in XXXX 2009, and could not have more children.
Each parent was to be sterilized, but each had medical problems. He had to pay a 20,000 Yuan deposit and she had to wear an IUD.

In late XXXX 2011, they tested themselves and found out she was pregnant, so they went into hiding before the next checkup in early XXXX 2011. They heard that a notice was left for them to attend the appointment, then another notice for abortion and sterilization, and a large fine, because they believed she was pregnant again. The home was damaged and they were ordered to pay a big fine.
After they left the male claimant's mother was detained for a week, and she developed asthma.

They did not disclose their route through USA to CBSA on instructions of the snakehead. They did not know Canada's immigration law, so they listened to the agent. Their lawyer in Canada told them to tell the truth, so they did The claimants had their third child in XXXX 2011, and she is pregnant again. They fear abortion, sterilization and a large fine.

The Panel finds the claimants not to be Convention refugees under Section 96, as they do not have a well-founded fear of persecution in China on any of the five Convention grounds.2 The Panel also finds that the claimants are not persons in need of protection under section 97 as, on a balance of probabilities; their removal to China would not subject them personally to a risk to life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture. 3 The Panel's reasons are as follows.

The Panel considered the issue of credibility. The Panel also considered whether the claimants require Canada's protection because of the potential application of the one child policy in China. The Panel applied the Gender Guidelines4.
The Panel has considered all of the evidence and submissions, including counsel's written submission, including of documents, dated March 4, 2014 (the "submission").

The claimant provided the oral testimony. The male claimant agreed with what his wife said, and declined to add anything. As the male claimant adopted what his wife said, and their PIF Narrative was joint, a negative credibility finding applies equally to both adult claimants. The minors were excused after being identified. Thus, as the claimant was found to be not credible, the claim fails with respect to all claimants. The Panel will note below that certain document(s) submitted will be found to be not genuine, and that redounds to negate the credibility of both adult claimants, as both will have been presumed to have submitted the false document(s). Thus, both adult claimants are found to be not credible. Identity

From the Chinese passports of all claimants in Exhibit R/A-2, the personal and national identities of these claimants are established.5 The Panel accepts from testimony the familial relationships alleged. Credibility

The claimant alleged she was wanted by authorities when she left China. However, she indicated that, despite this, the family was allowed to exit through Chinese exit controls. When asked how this was possible, she said the snakehead, or agent, arranged it for them. While this is technically possible, it is very unlikely. However, as this is in the nature of an implausibility only, the Panel will refrain from making a negative inference as to credibility from this.

The claimant alleged that she suffered two forced abortions between her first and second children. Had the Panel accepted this, then it is very possible her claim might have been accepted, for various reasons. However, for credibility reasons, the Panel does not accept this.

The translations of the certificates allegedly documenting these forced abortions are found on pp. 67 and 69 of Exhibit C-7. On p.69, the certificate in regard to the second procedure indicates the claimant to have been 31 years old on the date of the procedure, XXXX XXXX XXXX 2006. However, the claimant was born on XXXX XXXX, 1975 as per her passport. Therefore, she was 30, not 31, on XXXX XXXX, 2006, and the claimant was asked to explain this. She said it is Chinese custom or practice to enter in a document, say 31, if the patient is 30, or in her 31st year, as the claimant was then. However, it was pointed out to the claimant that on p.67, the certificate in regard to the second procedure indicates the claimant to have been 32 years old on the date of the procedure, XXXX XXXX XXXX 2007, and she in fact actually was 32 then, and 32, not 33, was entered. Thus, she was asked, why was this practice / custom only applied for once certificate, but not the other. Then she blamed this on mistake of the hospital. The Panel cannot accept this explanation. The claimant purports to rely on these documents to prove her claim, yet indicates they are not accurate, when challenged. This is the reason which causes the Panel to find these documents to be non-genuine. In making this finding that these documents are not genuine, the Panel notes that it is consistent with what is indicated in item 3.22 of Exhibit R/A-1, which references the proliferation of false documents emanating from China. A finding that a document is not genuine is sufficient to find the claimant, overall, to be not credible, and the Panel thus does so in this event.

From this also flows a finding that the female claimant did not suffer involuntary abortions, thus the claimants had much less of a reason to leave China. The Panel also for this reason will not apply the doctrine of Compelling Circumstances, as it conceivably could have considered, in that the Panel finds that the female claimant did not suffer two (or any) forced abortions as alleged.

The Panel also noted the address of the claimant on the abortion certificates, in an effort to see if they matched the address of the claimant as given in s.11 of her PIF. They did match the address given as of 2009. However, for some reason, the claimant omitted to indicate what her address was from 2001 to 2009, including what her address was in 2006 and 2007, the relevant times. The claimant could not explain why she did this, only to say that the family moved for some nine months in 2009. All this is somewhat odd, but the Panel will not make a negative inference as to credibility, but will note that an opportunity was foregone to validate the alleged genuineness of these certificates.

Many of the documents in Exhibit C-7, including the abortion certificates, were, as per the claimant, sent to her from China in 2012, and the envelope in which the documents were allegedly sent was shown at the hearing. However, the claimant arrived here in XXXX 2011, so, she was asked, why did she not bring these documents, valuable to prove her refugee claim, with her from China? Her answer was that she did not know they were necessary for her refugee claim, and she only got the idea when she spoke to her consultant in Canada. She said she only thought her passport was important (apparently the passports may not have been all that critical, though, since, she indicated, she had to turn them over to the agent in Canada, keeping only copies). This is unusual, and buttresses the finding above that the documents submitted are not genuine.

The allegation was made that the male claimant had medical issues, thus could not be sterilized. In support, a medical document for him was submitted, the translation being on p.51 of Exhibit C-7. It was divined at the hearing between counsel and the Panel that "chronic prostitutes" probably meant chronic prostate problems. The claimant explained that her husband had chronic prostate gland inflammation. Given that she said his problem was chronic, she was asked if he was taking any medication or medical attention for this condition in Canada, and she said it healed in China in 2011. However, as the problem was said to have been chronic, the Panel finds that it would have been unlikely to have been healed shortly before the claimants came to Canada. Thus, the Panel attaches this part of the medical documentation submitted, and by inference the other medical documentation, allegedly sent from China at the same time, to be of lesser weight, if it is even genuine. This analysis applies as well to the Notice of Sterilization, the English translation of which appears on p.63 of Exhibit C-7.

The issue of the claimant's addresses was re-visited. The claimant indicated that they hid, and changed residences, out of fear, in XXXX 2011. However, their PIF's. s.11, originally indicated that they moved, or hid, as of XXXX 2011, and, as per Exhibit C-6, submitted shortly before the hearing, they changed this to XXXX 2011. The claimant was asked why they originally indicated they moved in XXXX 2011, and all she could say was that it was a mistake. However, the Panel does not accept this explanation, given the other credibility concerns herein. The claimants confirmed when they signed their PIF's, and again at the outset of the hearing, that their PIF's were true, correct and complete, that they understood them, and that they were translated back into their language to them before they signed their PIF's. Notwithstanding this, the claimant now alleges that the PIF was in error. Considering the other credibility concerns herein, the panel makes a negative inference as to credibility from the variance between the original version of the PIF, and the amended version.

The claimant indicated in her PIF Narrative that, when the claimants were in hiding, the PSB came to their residence and left notices, and they were "ordered to pay a big fine". However, at the hearing, the claimant indicated they were not ordered to pay a fine. When questioned on the inconsistency, the claimant said it was verbal only. The Panel does not accept this explanation for the inconsistency, as it actually does not explain it, and, also, the Panel finds it implausible that a significant fine would be levied by means of a verbal notice only. The claimant has submitted other notices allegedly issued by the Chinese authorities to control and punish the claimants, yet contends that a significant fine was levelled, verbally only. This is not believable, and from this the Panel makes a negative inference as to credibility.
The claimant alleged that the PSB damaged their home, but could provide no documentary evidence that this was done, such as photos, invoices for replacement, repair, etc.

The above findings that the claimants have not been forthright are significantly fortified by the fact that the claimants, by their own admission, did not tell the truth to the Canadian authorities when they initially made their refugee claim in Canada. In Exhibit R/A-2, the Port of Entry (POE) Notes, the claimants indicated to CBSA that they flew directly for Hong Kong to Toronto. However, later, in the PIF, they changed their route to indicate that they flew from Hong Kong to Los Angeles, then to Seattle, then crossed illegally to BC, then flew domestically from Vancouver to Toronto. The claimant was asked why they made this false series of statements, and she said the agent advised them to do so.

The claimant confirmed she was over 30 years old when she took these actions, a mature adult and a mother. She understood that she told these falsehoods to the Government of Canada, the same institution from which she is now claiming protection against severe persecution in China. The Panel does not accept the claimant's explanation that she felt she had to listen to a smuggler, a criminal, even though the claimants may have had a payment dispute with the smuggler and the smuggler may have kept the originals of their passports, and even if she was pregnant, afraid and nervous as she says, and believed the smuggler gave her good advice as to what would be better for her refugee claim. They did not suggest the smuggler threatened them when they attended at Immigration, inland, in Toronto. Perhaps the claimants did not want to have to answer questions at their hearing about their failure to make an asylum claim in USA. The claimant said her counsel told her to ultimately tell the truth. More likely, the Panel finds, the claimants probably decided to "come clean" at the PIF stage because they noted what the CBSA agent inscribed in s.21, IMM 5611, in the POE Notes: "I.C.E. indicates that people with same names and DOB as our clients entered Los Angeles on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX11. Clients deny ever being to the U.S.", meaning they knew they would be caught on their lie. In any event, from this admitted lie to the Government of Canada the Panel makes a negative inference as to credibility. If the claimant does not tell the truth, then the Panel simply does not believe the claimant, nor should the Panel.

There was also an issue, as indicated above relating to subjective fear, or the lack thereof. The claimant indicated that the left China due to fear of abortion, sterilization, fines, etc. However, they belatedly admitted they were in USA for a number of days en route to Canada, but did not make an asylum claim during their sojourn there, despite USA being a signatory to the 1967 Protocol, and a country known for intaking and accepting a large number of asylum claimants. Again the claimant blamed this on her smuggler. However, as indicated, the claimant was a mature woman, allegedly seeking asylum for very serious reasons, yet she apparently bought passage to Canada and went there, passing up an opportunity to claim in USA. In so doing, pregnant as she was and scared as she said she was, she allegedly performed an illegal hike over an unfamiliar international boundary, risking apprehension, detention and potential removal to China on the way. The Panel finds that this behaviour indicated that the claimant did not have a real, or genuine, fear of a return to China as alleged. Further, in that she alleged that she did, from this the panel makes a negative inference as to credibility. The Panel finds that the claimant was simply asylum shopping, or, in the alternative, embarked on a deliberate plan to get her entire family to Canada, for whatever reason.

From all the above credibility issues, the Panel finds that the claimant's evidence has been, overall, not credible, and thus insufficient to support the claimants' claim for refugee protection. The One-Child Policy

The claimants came to Canada in XXXX 2011. They have had one child here, a Canadian citizen now, and are expecting another future Canadian citizen child in XXXX 2014. Counsel indicated that this child will be born in Canada, and the Panel agrees. The claimants now claim that the claimant will be persecuted if she returns to China with two Canadian children in addition to her two Chinese children. The Panel acknowledges that t
here is some possibility of persecution in China in some circumstances if Chinese citizens have more than one child in China, or two in the case of the claimant.

However, these circumstances are, the Panel finds, unlikely to apply to the claimants. The Panel has found, for credibility reasons, that the state did not force the claimant to undergo any abortions. It is conceivable that such could have occurred to a person with the female claimant's profile, but the Panel finds that it did not occur to her.

Further, the claimant will now have had four children, and while they claim they love children and want more, it would not appear necessarily likely that the couple will wish to have more children (Probably apropos of nothing, the Panel notes the claimant is 38 and her husband 34 as of the hearing, which would appear somewhat unusual). The female claimant is, as noted, 38 years old, and it may be less likely than otherwise that China will enforce sterilization on a female citizen relatively close to the end of her child-bearing years. However, the above is speculation only, and the Panel does not rely on it. It is also possible that if the claimants do leave Canada, they may decide to leave their Canadian children in Canada, in which event they would have only the two Chinese children in China, and would thus not fall afoul of the one-child policy. However, again, the Panel does not rely on this factor in making its decision. Also not directly considered by the Panel is that in the hypothetical event children 3 and 4, the Canadian citizens, were brought to China by the adults (if China would even accept them as immigrants), then any problems they would hypothetically face could be said to not be the direct concern of the Panel, as these children are not refugee claimants before the Board, and thus are not directly entitled to Canada's refugee protection.

Counsel went to great efforts to point out to the Panel that the one-child policy would be fully in force against the claimants, regardless of the factors noted in the immediately preceding paragraph, and more importantly, regardless of the fact that children 3 and 4 would have been born outside China. She pointed out documentation which specifically indicates that in Guangdong Province, where the claimants are from and where they presumably would go to, the draconian policies of sterilization, abortion, serious fines, etc., apply to families where children are born outside China.

Thus, the Panel would have to agree with counsel that such is the state of the law. However, the Panel also needs to consider whether the law is actually being enforced. In this regard, the Panel notes item 5.1 of Exhibit R/A-1, CHN103033.E, which indicates as follows: In general, people who return to China from abroad are actively welcomed back to the "motherland" and children born outside China largely forgiven ... Chinese couples living abroad are not bound to the one-child policy. Chinese citizens studying or working in foreign countries can return with more than one child without any serious problem ... Chinese nationals who have children while abroad may not be subject to the one-child policy ... there is an emerging class of rich Chinese citizens who simply pay a fine or travel overseas to have additional children.6

It thus appears as if, despite the letter of the law, the claimants would not be persecuted in China if they hypothetically returned there, and decided to take children 3 and 4 there and make the necessary efforts to allow these Canadian citizen children to gain entry to China, and the right to live there, and the Panel so finds. Thus, the Panel finds, there is not even a serious possibility that any of the claimants would be persecuted in China, as these restrictive laws and policies would not apply to them.

For credibility reasons, the Panel has found that the claimants were not persecuted in China in the past. They submitted at least one false document, and admittedly made a significant untruth to CBSA. Thus, they are simply not believed unless their statements are evidently true, such as, as counsel pointed out, they will soon have four children. The Panel thus does not accept that the claimant was persecuted as she said in the past, whether because she submitted false documents to bolster her claim, or perhaps the authorities did not persecute her for enforcement variability reasons, which the documentation before the Panel indicates often applies in this issue in China. For this reason, the Panel does not accept that the Family Planning Office is looking for the claimant or has a file on her, as she alleges. For reasons noted above, the Panel also does not accept that any claimant will be persecuted in China upon a hypothetical return there.

As a result of the above findings, the Panel finds the claimants to not be Convention refugees under section 96, nor persons in need of protection under section 97 of the IRPA. As such, for the reasons noted above, the claim is rejected with respect to all the claimants. (signed) 'M. Sterlin' M.
